title: Fabricius Warns Pyrrhus of Poison
text:
In 280 and 279 BC King Pyrrhus of Epirus invaded Italy to help the Greek city of Tarentum against Rome, and won two costly battles. Plutarch says the Roman envoy Gaius Fabricius impressed Pyrrhus deeply: he refused the king's offers of gold and could not be startled even when Pyrrhus had an elephant suddenly trumpet behind him.

The next year Fabricius was consul. According to Plutarch, a man came to the Roman camp with a letter from the king's own physician, offering to poison Pyrrhus and end the war if Rome paid him well. Fabricius was disgusted. With his fellow consul he wrote to Pyrrhus to warn him. The letter told the king he seemed to judge badly both his friends and his enemies, since he was at war with honest men and trusted villains. The Romans added that they were not telling him out of favor, but so that no one could say Rome had won by treachery because it could not win by force.

Pyrrhus investigated, punished the physician and sent his Roman prisoners home without ransom. Rome, not wanting to be in his debt, freed an equal number of his allies' prisoners in return.
lesson: Win honestly, even against an enemy. Refusing a dirty shortcut protects your own name, and decency can earn more from an opponent than betrayal ever would.
people: Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, Quintus Aemilius Papus, Pyrrhus of Epirus
caveat: Ancient writers tell different versions of the plot and the traitor's identity.
